definition: To become aware of or discover information about something.
etymology: From learn, meaning to gain knowledge, + of, indicating the subject of knowledge.

definition: To speak angrily to someone because they have done something wrong.
etymology: From Middle English scolden, meaning to rebuke or reprimand.

definition: To speak angrily to someone because they have done something wrong.
etymology: From tell + off, developing the figurative meaning of reprimanding someone.

definition: Specific or relating to one specific person, thing, or situation.
etymology: From Latin particularis, meaning relating to a part or individual.

definition: Clearly defined, identified, or related to a particular thing.
etymology: From Latin specificus, meaning constituting a species or kind.

definition: Not able to be relied upon or trusted.
etymology: From un- (not) + rely + -able (capable of).

definition: Different from what is normal, common, or expected.
etymology: From un- (not) + usual (common or customary).

definition: Not common or occurring infrequently.
etymology: From Latin rarus, meaning thin, sparse, or uncommon.

definition: To give something a particular form or influence how something develops.
etymology: From Old English sceap, meaning form or shape.

definition: To create, develop, or bring something into existence.
etymology: From Latin formare, meaning to shape or form.

definition: A long, narrow opening or crack in a surface, especially in rock.
etymology: From Latin fissura, meaning a cleft or crack, from findere, meaning to split.

definition: The power or skill to do something successfully.
etymology: From Latin habilitas, meaning ability or fitness.

definition: To explain something or represent a particular amount or proportion.
etymology: From account, meaning a report or explanation, + for.

definition: The practical value or usefulness of something.
etymology: From Latin utilitas, meaning usefulness or advantage.

definition: A tool or device used for a particular purpose, especially scientific or technical work.
etymology: From Latin instrumentum, meaning tool or equipment.

definition: A series of connected things, events, or processes.
etymology: From Old French chaine, from Latin catena, meaning chain.

definition: In a basic or fundamental way; describing the main nature of something.
etymology: From essential + -ly, from Latin essentia, meaning being or essence.

definition: Needed for a particular purpose or situation.
etymology: From Latin necessarius, meaning indispensable or unavoidable.

definition: Completely necessary or extremely important.
etymology: From Latin essentialis, meaning relating to essence or being.

definition: To divide or keep things apart; existing independently.
etymology: From Latin separare, meaning to divide or set apart.

definition: As a result or in this way.
etymology: From Old English þus, meaning in this way.

definition: For that reason; as a result.
etymology: From Old English þærfore, meaning for that reason.

definition: Used to emphasize that something is even less likely, possible, or true than something already mentioned.
etymology: A combination of much and the comparative form less, used as an emphatic expression.

definition: The ability to adapt to different activities, purposes, or situations.
etymology: From Latin versatilis, meaning turning easily or adaptable.

definition: The ability to adjust effectively to new conditions or situations.
etymology: From adaptable + -ity, from adapt, meaning to adjust to new conditions.

definition: The smallest amount, number, or degree possible or allowed.
etymology: From Latin minimum, meaning the smallest.

definition: Far away in space or time.
etymology: From Latin distant-, meaning standing apart or being remote.

definition: To get, acquire, or receive something, especially through effort or a particular process.
etymology: From Latin obtinere, meaning to acquire or gain possession of.

definition: To become worse in quality, condition, or effectiveness.
etymology: From Latin deteriorare, meaning to make worse or become worse.

definition: To become or make something smaller, weaker, or less important.
etymology: From Latin diminuere, meaning to make smaller.

definition: The ability or power to do something successfully.
etymology: From capable + -ity, ultimately from Latin capabilis, meaning able to contain or receive.

definition: In the same order as the people or things previously mentioned.
etymology: From respective + -ly, from Latin respectivus, meaning relating to each separately.

definition: To remember something or bring a past event or fact back into the mind.
etymology: From re- (back) + call, meaning to call back.

definition: To use knowledge, experience, or resources as a source of help or information.
etymology: From draw, meaning to take or pull, + on, developing the figurative sense of using a resource.

definition: To use something effectively for a particular purpose.
etymology: From French utiliser, from Latin utilis, meaning useful.

definition: Relating to the meaning of words, phrases, or other linguistic expressions.
etymology: From Greek sēmantikos, meaning significant or relating to meaning.

definition: The total amount resulting from adding numbers or quantities together.
etymology: From Latin summa, meaning highest or total amount.

definition: Quickly and without delay.
etymology: From prompt + -ly, from Latin promptus, meaning ready or immediate.

definition: An event, incident, or instance of something happening.
etymology: From occur + -ence, from Latin occurrere, meaning to happen or come about.

definition: The complete amount or number of something; to add up to a complete amount.
etymology: From Latin totalis, meaning whole or complete.

definition: To obtain something or develop a skill, quality, or habit over time.
etymology: From Latin acquirere, meaning to gain or obtain.

translations.ru: в наше время; в наши дни

definition: At the present time or in the current period.
etymology: From now + a days, originally referring to the present period.

definition: The group or system responsible for controlling and administering a country or region.
etymology: From govern + -ment, from Latin gubernare, meaning to steer or rule.

definition: Not responsible for a crime or wrongdoing; not guilty.
etymology: From Latin innocens, meaning harmless or not guilty.

definition: To suggest that something is true or exists without stating it directly.
etymology: From Latin implicare, meaning to involve or entangle.

definition: To attract someone by offering something appealing, often in order to persuade or deceive them.
etymology: From Old French loirre, meaning a bait or attraction.

definition: To trick someone into giving money, information, or something else of value.
etymology: Shortened from confidence trick and ultimately confidence man.

definition: To copy the actions, behavior, or appearance of someone or something.
etymology: From Latin imitari, meaning to copy or reproduce.

definition: Having the greatest amount of wealth among a group.
etymology: From wealth + -y, meaning possessing wealth.

definition: To calculate or judge approximately the size, value, amount, or cost of something.
etymology: From Latin aestimare, meaning to value or assess.

definition: A detailed examination or inquiry into a subject, event, or situation.
etymology: From Latin investigatio, from investigare, meaning to trace or search into.

definition: To make something previously unknown or hidden known to others.
etymology: From Latin revelare, meaning to uncover or disclose.

definition: More importantly than anything else; especially.
etymology: A phrase formed from above, meaning higher in importance, + all.

definition: To identify someone or something from previous knowledge or to acknowledge something as true or important.
etymology: From Latin recognoscere, meaning to know again.

definition: To be careful because something may be dangerous, deceptive, or problematic.
etymology: Wary comes from Old English wær, meaning cautious or aware.

definition: Requiring immediate attention or action.
etymology: From Latin urgere, meaning to press or drive.

definition: Causing sadness, worry, or emotional distress.
etymology: From upset + -ing, describing something that causes emotional disturbance.

definition: A person or organization that receives something.
etymology: From Latin recipiens, meaning receiving, from recipere, meaning to receive.

definition: Legally or officially acceptable, or based on sound reasoning and evidence.
etymology: From Latin validus, meaning strong, effective, or legally binding.

definition: Allowed or required by law.
etymology: From Latin legalis, meaning relating to the law.

definition: Showing bravery and the ability to face danger, difficulty, or pain.
etymology: From courage + -ous, from Old French corage, meaning heart or spirit.

definition: Feeling embarrassed or guilty because of something wrong or dishonorable.
etymology: From Old English a-scamod, meaning filled with shame.

definition: Used to introduce an additional point that supports or strengthens what has just been said.
etymology: From more + over, meaning in addition.

definition: Used to add another point that supports or develops the previous statement.
etymology: From further + more, meaning in addition or additionally.

definition: Used to refer to any person, regardless of who they are.
etymology: From who + ever, indicating an unrestricted person.

definition: A dishonest, immoral, or unpleasant person.
etymology: Origin uncertain; recorded in English since the 16th century.

definition: To speak in a quiet, unclear voice, often because of anger or dissatisfaction.
etymology: Probably imitative in origin, representing a low indistinct sound.

definition: To speak very quietly or make a low continuous sound.
etymology: From Latin murmurare, imitating a low continuous sound.

definition: To take and hold something firmly; to understand something completely.
etymology: From Middle English graspen, meaning to seize or hold.

definition: Past participle of tear; damaged by pulling apart or splitting.
etymology: From Old English teran, meaning to pull apart or rend.

definition: To look steadily and intently at someone or something.
etymology: From Middle English gazen, meaning to look steadily.

definition: To suddenly lose consciousness for a short period.
etymology: From Old French feindre, later associated with loss of strength or consciousness.

definition: A physical or mental ability to perceive or understand something.
etymology: From Latin sensus, meaning perception or feeling.

definition: To extend or spread something over a greater distance or area.
etymology: From Old English streccan, meaning to stretch or extend.

definition: To save someone or something from danger, harm, or difficulty.
etymology: From Old French rescoure, meaning to recover or save.

definition: To move something down or reduce its level, amount, or intensity.
etymology: From lower, related to low, meaning to make or become lower.

definition: In a way that requires immediate attention or action.
etymology: From urgent + -ly, from Latin urgere, meaning to press or drive.

definition: Showing a lack of courage when facing danger or difficulty.
etymology: From coward + -ly, meaning like a coward.

definition: A strong feeling of appreciation for something received or done by someone.
etymology: From Latin gratitudo, meaning thankfulness or gratefulness.

definition: To be useful for a particular purpose or to perform a particular function.
etymology: From Latin servire, meaning to serve or be useful.

definition: To make a serious promise or statement, especially by making an oath.
etymology: From Old English swerian, meaning to take an oath.

definition: A statement that someone will definitely do or provide something, or the act of making such a statement.
etymology: From Latin promittere, meaning to send forth or assure beforehand.

definition: Extreme anger or violent uncontrolled emotion.
etymology: From Old French rage, from Latin rabies, meaning madness or fury.

definition: To make a serious and formal promise.
etymology: From Old French vou, from Latin votum, meaning a solemn promise.

definition: To move into a position in which one or both knees are on the ground.
etymology: From Old English cnēowlian, meaning to kneel.

definition: To stop someone while they are speaking or to stop a process temporarily.
etymology: From Latin interrumpere, meaning to break apart or interrupt.

definition: In a way that shows jealousy or envy.
etymology: From jealous + -ly, from Old French gelos.

definition: A place or point through which someone enters a building or area.
etymology: From enter + -ance, from Latin intrare, meaning to go into.

definition: Lit or illuminated by candles.
etymology: A compound of candle + lit.

definition: A state of extreme irrationality, uncontrolled behavior, or mental disturbance.
etymology: From mad + -ness, describing a state of being mad.

definition: A meeting or group of people who come together for a particular purpose.
etymology: From gather + -ing, meaning an act or occasion of gathering.

definition: To cry with short, uneven breaths, usually because of strong emotion.
etymology: Probably imitative in origin, representing the sound of crying.
